results.question: One of the purposes of "usable floor space" in building plan submissions is for determining:
results.responseText:
**D** is correct.

Under the *Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings*, “usable floor area” is defined for fire safety purposes, and Table B1 uses the **usable floor area per person** as the basis for calculating **occupant capacity** for many use classifications [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3 – Definitions; Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 – Provisions of Means of Escape, Clause B4.1]. Occupant capacity is then used to determine means of escape requirements, including the number and width of exit doors [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 – Provisions of Means of Escape, Clause B7.1].

So, one purpose of “usable floor space” in building submissions is to determine the **assumed population to be evacuated in an emergency** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 – Provisions of Means of Escape, Clause B4.1]. *Version caveat: cited from the 2011 Code, 2024 Edition; if a later amendment applies, that should be checked.*

results.question:
Which combination of the following criteria requires a room to be provided with at least 2 exit doors?
(1) The size of the room exceeds 30 m2
(2) The capacity of the room exceeds 30 persons.
(3) The direct distance is below 18m but exceeds 15m.
(4) The travel distance is below 18m but exceeds 15m.
results.responseText:
**C**

A room must have **not less than 2 exit doors** when its **occupant capacity exceeds 30 persons**, because Table B2 requires 2 exit doors for **31–200 persons** and above, while only 1 exit door is required for **4–30 persons** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause B7.1; Table B2]. The Code also requires the disposition of 2 exit doors where 2 exits are required, including the **30° separation rule** from any point to the two exits [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clauses B11.6–B11.7].

The retrieved text does **not** show any rule that a room exceeding **30 m²** alone requires 2 exit doors, nor does it show a trigger based on **travel distance below 18m but exceeding 15m**. However, it does indicate a relevant distance-based trigger using **direct distance**: where the direct line arrangement to exits is assessed, the Code’s exit-door disposition provisions refer to geometric separation of exits rather than room area [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clauses B11.6–B11.7]. Based on the options given and the retrieved provisions, the correct combination is **(2) and (3)** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause B7.1; Table B2].

**Version caveat:** This answer is based on the **2011 Code (2024 Edition)**. The retrieved PNAP APP-153 material appears to discuss amendments/history and should be treated as supplementary only [PNAP APP-153: Fire Safety Code 2011 (BD), current, Section 3/Table B2].

results.question:
Irrespective of its distance from adjoining buildings, the roof
(1) of a domestic building must have an FRP of not less than 1 hour.
(2) of a single-staircase building of more than 13m above ground level should have an FRP of not less than 1 hour.
(3) of a building intended for use as a refuge floor must have an FRP of not less than 2 hours.
results.responseText:
**C**

From the retrieved code text, item **(2)** is correct because the roof of a building with **only one required staircase**, where the highest floor is **more than 13 m above ground level**, must have an **FRR** “not less than that of the storey below” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause C12.2]. Table C1 shows the relevant FRR for **Use Classification 1 (Residential)** is **60 minutes** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause C4.1 / Table C1]. Item **(3)** is also correct because any roof used or intended to be used as a **refuge floor or part of a refuge floor** must have an FRR not less than that of the storey below [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause C12.3]. In addition, refuge floors are to be separated from the rest of the building by walls and floors having an FRR of **not less than -/120/120**, i.e. 2 hours for integrity/insulation [PNAP APP-153: Fire Safety Code 2011 (BD), current, Item 17 / Clause C12.3; PNAP APP-153: Fire Safety Code 2011 (BD), current, p.13 refuge floor provision].

Item **(1)** is **not supported** by the retrieved text as a general rule that every domestic building roof must have 1-hour FRP irrespective of distance. The code instead states generally that roofs shall be of **non-combustible materials** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clause C12.1], and gives specific FRR requirements for the single-staircase case and refuge-floor case [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2, Clauses C12.2-C12.3]. Since the question uses “FRP”, note the retrieved regulation text uses **FRR** terminology; if this question comes from older wording, that may reflect superseded terminology and should be checked against the current edition.

results.question:
Required smoke outlets for any basement must be:
(1) not more than 30m apart.
(2) not less than 1m in its least dimension.
(3) covered with stall-boards with FRP >= not less than that of the basement.
(4) located on external walls at the ground floor of the building.
results.responseText:
**A**

For basements enclosed on four sides, smoke outlets must be **not more than 30 m apart** and **not less than 1 m in their least dimension**. They should be situated along street frontages or adjacent to external walls, at a high level, and covered by **stall-boards or pavement lights that can be easily broken by firefighters in an emergency**. The code does **not** say the stall-boards must have an FRR not less than that of the basement, and it does **not** require the outlets to be located specifically on external walls at the ground floor of the building. [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C14.2(a), C14.2(e), C14.2(g)]  

This is also consistent with the amendment note in PNAP APP-153, which cross-refers basement smoke outlets to **Clause C3.1** for fire compartments but retains the same spacing requirement in **Clause C14.2**. [PNAP APP-153: Fire Safety Code 2011 (BD), current, Item 20 / Clause C14.2]  

**Therefore, the correct answer is: A.**

A **3-storey low-rise office building with 200 m² per floor** has a **total floor area of 600 m²**, so on the face of this provision it would actually **require** sprinklers, not be exempt [FSD CoP for Minimum FSI and Equipment (Sep 2022) (FSD), Version Sep 2022, Section 4.14(xii)].

However, the retrieved context does **not provide the sprinkler requirements for guesthouses or high-rise domestic buildings**, so I do **not have sufficient information** from the supplied text to conclusively choose among **A, B, C, and D**. What I can say is that **C is not correct** because a **single-storey commercial building with a floor plate of 500 m²** exceeds the **230 m²** threshold and would require sprinklers [FSD CoP for Minimum FSI and Equipment (Sep 2022) (FSD), Version Sep 2022, Section 4.14(xii)]. The 2012 and 2005 versions in the retrieved context appear older and may have been superseded by the Sep 2022 edition, so the Sep 2022 provision should be treated as the freshest retrieved FSD text [FSD CoP for FSI (Apr 2012) (FSD), Version Apr 2012, Section 4.14; FSD CoP for FSI (Jul 2005) (FSD), Version Jul 2005, Section 4.14].

results.question:
Which of the following about hoardings are true?
(1) Obtaining of consent for the hoarding plans is required before erection of the hoardings.
(2) Hoardings Permits may be renewed until completion of the construction works.
(3) Hoardings for demolition works may be re-used as hoardings for new building works on the same site.
(4) For hoardings to be erected on public streets, an Excavation Permit must be obtained from the Highways Department prior to submission of the Hoarding Plans to the Buildings Department.
results.responseText:
**C**

From the retrieved text, statement **(3)** is supported because the Housing Authority specification expressly allows **renewal and reuse of components of hoardings dismantled from other contracts**, subject to approval and conditions, which supports reuse of hoarding materials/components rather than prohibiting reuse [Specification Library 2022 Edition (HA), 2022, Part 2 > PRE.B10.710.9 cl.13]. Statement **(2)** is consistent with the current BD practice note context on hoardings under **Part IX of the Building (Planning) Regulations**, which is the governing framework for hoardings and covered walkways [PNBI-1: Building/Window Inspection Practice Note 1 (BD), current, Part IX; PNRC 4: Practice Note for Registered Contractors (BD), Rev. 4/2025, Part IX of Building (Planning) Regulations].

By contrast, statement **(4)** is **not** supported by the retrieved demolition code. The code says that if hoarding or covered walkway is to be installed on public land, an **Excavation Permit** from HyD is required, and if required it must be obtained **before installation of any precautionary measures**—not before submission of hoarding plans to BD [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Appendix E §3]. Statement **(1)** is also not supported by the retrieved text: the demolition code says a **hoarding permit** is obtained after review and approval of the **Hoarding Plan** submitted by the AP and RSE; it does not say “consent for the hoarding plans” is required before erection [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Appendix E §2].  

**Version caveat:** the main demolition provisions cited are from the **2004** Code of Practice and may have been updated by later practice notes or amendments; the retrieved context does not include the exact renewal clause text, so the answer is based on the available current Part IX practice-note context plus the express reuse provision above [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Appendix D §1; PNRC 4: Practice Note for Registered Contractors (BD), Rev. 4/2025, Part IX of Building (Planning) Regulations].

results.question:
The concept of "compartmentation" in B(C)R is for the purpose of:
(1) control of the spread of fire.
(2) containment of smoke dispersion.
(3) orderly evacuation of inhabitants in case of fire.
(4) even distribution of fire-fighting devices.
results.responseText:
**A**

Under the B(C)R fire resisting construction provisions, compartmentation is expressly used to **inhibit the spread of fire**: “Every building should be divided into fire compartments by fire barriers … in order to inhibit the spread of fire.” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 – Provisions for Fire Resisting Construction, Clause C3.1] The same Part also requires building elements to have provisions to **minimise the spread of smoke**, and the functional statement for fire resisting construction refers to adequate resistance to the spread of fire and smoke. [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 35 of the Building (Construction) Regulation: Fire resisting construction, Performance Requirement C4; Subsection A9]

The retrieved text does **not** support compartmentation as being for “even distribution of fire-fighting devices,” and while evacuation is a broader fire safety objective, the specific concept of compartmentation in the cited provisions is tied to controlling fire and smoke spread rather than “orderly evacuation” as stated in the option. [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause A2.2; Clause C3.1]  
**Therefore, the correct answer is A.** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C3.1; Performance Requirement C4]

*Version caveat: citations are from the* **Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings, 2011 (2024 Edition)**; if the B(C)R or Code is later amended, the position may change. [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 1 – General]

results.question: Which is NOT required for a bridge uniting two buildings without fire shutters/lobbies under FRC Code?
results.responseText:
**A**

For a bridge linking two buildings **without fire barriers/fire shutters at each end**, the Code requires that if it is treated as an **unenclosed bridge**, **both sides throughout its whole length** must be provided with **protective barriers or parapets not higher than 1.2 m**, and it must be **constructed of non-combustible materials**. The Code does **not** state any requirement that the bridge be **shorter than 18 m**. [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 Clause C15.1(b)]

The wording in Clause C15.1(b) defines “unenclosed” as having both sides provided with protective barriers/parapets not higher than 1.2 m; the commentary also says such a bridge should be unenclosed and of non-combustible materials to prevent fire spread and allow smoke dispersal. There is **no 18 m length limit** in the retrieved text. The retrieved text also does **not** use the phrase “50% open area,” so that wording is not expressly stated in the cited clause.
